prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Exemplary road and engine noise control systems and methods include directly picking up road noise from a structural element of a vehicle to generate a first sense signal representative of the road noise, directly picking up engine noise from an engine of the vehicle to generate a second sense signal representative of the engine noise, and combining the first sense signal and the second sense signal to provide a combination signal representing the combination of the first sense signal and the second sense signal. The systems and methods further include broadband active noise control filtering to generate a filtered combination signal from the combination signal, converting the filtered combination signal provided by the active noise control filtering into anti-noise and radiating the anti-noise to a listening position in an interior of the vehicle. The filtered combination signal is configured so that the anti-noise reduces the noise at the listening position.

Example systems and techniques for controlling road and engine noise involve sensing road noise directly from a vehicle structural component to produce a first detection signal corresponding to that road noise, and sensing engine noise directly from the vehicle engine to produce a second detection signal corresponding to that engine noise. The first and second detection signals are then combined to create a combined signal that represents both signals together.

The systems and techniques also use broadband active noise control filtering to process the combined signal and generate a filtered combined signal. This filtered combined signal is converted into anti-noise, which is emitted toward a listening location inside the vehicle. The filtered combined signal is arranged so that the resulting anti-noise decreases the noise heard at that listening location.

The system is configured to reduce noise inside a vehicle by addressing multiple noise sources in a coordinated manner. In operation, the system directly detects road noise from a structural element of the vehicle, such as a suspension component, chassis member, or another vehicle structure that carries vibrations caused by contact between the tires and the road surface. This detection produces a road noise signal that represents noise and vibration associated with road input.

The system also directly detects engine noise from the vehicle’s engine. For example, one or more sensors may monitor vibrations, acoustic energy, rotational behavior, or other engine-related characteristics. Based on this detection, the system generates an engine noise signal that represents noise produced by operation of the engine.

The road noise signal and the engine noise signal are then combined to form a single combined signal. This combined signal represents both road noise and engine noise, allowing the system to process the two noise sources together rather than treating them entirely separately.

The combined signal is provided to a broadband active noise control filter. The broadband active noise control filtering processes the combined signal over a range of frequencies and generates a filtered signal suitable for reducing the detected noise components. The filtering may account for the acoustic path between the noise sources, the loudspeakers, and one or more listening positions within the vehicle cabin.

The filtered signal is then converted into anti-noise by one or more acoustic transducers, such as loudspeakers located inside the vehicle. The anti-noise is radiated into the passenger compartment and is arranged to interfere destructively with the road noise and engine noise at a listening position, such as near an occupant’s ears. As a result, the perceived noise level inside the vehicle is reduced.

The described vehicle noise control approach is designed to improve acoustic comfort inside a vehicle cabin by actively reducing unwanted noise before it becomes objectionable to occupants. In operation, the system detects multiple major sources of interior noise, including road-induced noise and engine-related noise. Road noise is sensed directly from a structural element of the vehicle, such as a suspension component, chassis member, body panel, or other part that transmits vibration caused by tire contact with the road surface. Engine noise is detected from the engine or an engine-associated component, allowing the system to capture sound or vibration related to engine operation, combustion, rotation, and load changes.

The signals obtained from these sensing points are supplied to a controller that processes them together. By combining information from both the road-noise sensor and the engine-noise sensor, the controller can form a more complete representation of the noise that is likely to enter the passenger compartment. This combined signal is then processed using broadband active noise control filtering. Unlike a system that targets only a narrow frequency or a single tonal component, broadband filtering is capable of addressing a wider range of frequencies, making it suitable for complex vehicle noise that may vary with speed, road surface, engine speed, and driving conditions.

After the control signal has been generated, it is converted into acoustic anti-noise by one or more sound-producing devices, such as loudspeakers located in the vehicle cabin. The anti-noise is radiated into the passenger compartment in a controlled manner so that it interferes destructively with the unwanted noise at one or more listening positions, such as near the ears of the driver or passengers. By producing a sound field that is substantially opposite in phase to the incoming noise, the system reduces the perceived noise level within the cabin.

As a result, occupants experience a quieter and more comfortable interior environment. The approach is particularly useful because it accounts for both structural road noise and engine noise, two significant contributors to cabin sound levels. By sensing these noise sources close to their origin and applying active broadband filtering, the system can respond effectively to changing operating conditions and provide improved noise reduction across a range of driving situations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style abstract for a vehicle system that combines road noise sensing and engine noise sensing, applies broadband active noise control filtering, and outputs anti-noise inside the cabin.
counterfactuals.output: A vehicle noise control system includes a plurality of sensors configured to detect road-induced noise and engine-induced noise associated with operation of a vehicle. The system further includes a controller configured to receive road noise signals and engine noise signals from the plurality of sensors, generate one or more broadband active noise control signals by applying adaptive filtering to the received signals, and produce anti-noise signals corresponding to noise components within a vehicle cabin. One or more acoustic transducers disposed in the cabin output the anti-noise signals to attenuate broadband noise perceived by occupants. The controller may combine feedforward inputs associated with wheel, suspension, body, powertrain, or engine vibration with error signals from cabin microphones to adaptively update the filtering and improve cancellation of both road noise and engine noise under changing vehicle operating conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise technical description of systems and methods for reducing both road noise and engine noise in a vehicle using directly sensed signals and active noise cancellation.
counterfactuals.output:
A vehicle noise-reduction system includes an active noise cancellation controller configured to attenuate both road-induced noise and engine-order noise within a passenger cabin using directly sensed reference signals.

The system may include one or more vibration or acceleration sensors mounted to vehicle structures that carry road inputs, such as suspension components, wheel hubs, subframes, body attachment points, or chassis members. These sensors directly measure road-induced vibration before or as it propagates into the cabin. The system may also include engine-related sensors, such as a crankshaft position sensor, tachometer signal, cylinder firing signal, motor torque signal, or powertrain mount accelerometer, to provide direct reference information representative of engine noise or engine-order vibration.

A controller receives the road-noise reference signals and engine-noise reference signals and generates anti-noise signals using adaptive filtering. The controller may implement feedforward active noise control, in which reference signals are filtered through adaptive filters corresponding to cabin acoustic transfer paths. Error microphones positioned in the cabin provide residual noise feedback, allowing the controller to update filter coefficients to minimize acoustic pressure at one or more occupant locations.

The controller may process road-noise and engine-noise references in separate or combined control paths. Road-noise control may use broadband adaptive filters driven by suspension or body acceleration signals, while engine-noise control may use narrowband or order-based filters synchronized to engine speed or firing events. The resulting anti-noise signals are summed and output through one or more loudspeakers of the vehicle audio system or dedicated actuators to generate acoustic waves that destructively interfere with road and engine noise in the cabin.

Methods include directly sensing road vibration and engine operating signals, estimating corresponding cabin noise components, adaptively generating cancellation signals, reproducing the cancellation signals through vehicle speakers, measuring residual cabin noise with microphones, and continuously updating control parameters to reduce both broadband road noise and tonal engine noise under changing driving conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an exemplary patent claim summary describing how structural road noise pickup and engine noise pickup are combined into one signal for broadband ANC in a vehicle interior.
counterfactuals.output:
**Exemplary Patent Claim Summary**

A vehicle active noise control system is configured to reduce broadband noise within a vehicle interior by combining multiple noise-related pickup signals into a single reference signal for use by an adaptive noise cancellation controller. The system includes one or more structural road-noise sensors mechanically coupled to a vehicle body, suspension component, subframe, wheel assembly, or other structure that conducts vibration caused by tire-road interaction. The system further includes one or more engine-noise pickup devices configured to detect engine-related vibration, acoustic pressure, rotational order information, or powertrain operating characteristics associated with engine noise transmitted into the passenger compartment.

Signals from the structural road-noise pickup and the engine-noise pickup are conditioned and combined to form a composite broadband reference signal. The conditioning may include filtering, gain scaling, phase adjustment, delay compensation, frequency-band allocation, normalization, weighting based on vehicle operating state, or adaptive mixing. The composite reference signal represents both road-induced structural noise and engine-induced noise components over a broadband frequency range.

An active noise cancellation controller receives the composite reference signal and generates one or more anti-noise control signals using an adaptive filter algorithm. The anti-noise signals are supplied to one or more loudspeakers positioned in the vehicle interior to produce sound that destructively interferes with road noise and engine noise at one or more occupant listening positions. One or more error microphones within the cabin provide residual noise signals to the controller, enabling adaptive updating of the filter coefficients to minimize broadband interior noise.

In one implementation, the structural road-noise pickup provides high-bandwidth vibration information correlated with tire-road excitation, while the engine-noise pickup provides engine-order or combustion-related information correlated with powertrain noise. A signal combiner merges these inputs into a unified reference channel, allowing a single broadband ANC processing path to address both road noise and engine noise without requiring separate independent cancellation systems. The relative contribution of each pickup signal may be dynamically adjusted according to vehicle speed, engine speed, gear state, acceleration, road surface condition, or cabin acoustic response.

The claimed concept therefore encompasses a broadband vehicle ANC architecture in which structurally sensed road-noise information and engine-noise information are jointly processed into one composite reference signal that drives adaptive anti-noise generation for reducing combined road and engine noise in the vehicle interior.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an automotive active noise control method where road noise is sensed from a vehicle structural element, engine noise is sensed from the engine, the signals are combined, filtered, and radiated as anti-noise to a listening position.
counterfactuals.output:
An automotive active noise control method can be implemented as follows:

Road-induced vibration/noise is detected by a sensor mounted on a vehicle structural element, such as a suspension member, body frame, chassis component, or other structure that transmits road noise into the passenger compartment. Separately, engine-related noise or vibration is detected by a sensor associated with the engine, such as an engine vibration sensor, tachometer-derived signal, crankshaft sensor, or microphone/vibration pickup positioned to sense engine noise.

The road-noise signal and the engine-noise signal are supplied to a controller. The controller combines these input signals to form a composite reference signal representing noise components expected at a listening position in the vehicle cabin. The combined signal is then processed through one or more adaptive or fixed filters. These filters shape the amplitude, phase, and frequency content of the signal so that, when reproduced acoustically, it corresponds to an inverse or canceling waveform of the unwanted noise at the listening position.

The filtered cancellation signal is output to one or more loudspeakers located in the vehicle interior. The loudspeakers radiate anti-noise toward the listening position, such as the driver’s or passenger’s ear location. At the listening position, the anti-noise destructively interferes with the road noise and engine noise, reducing the perceived sound level. Optionally, an error microphone near the listening position may monitor the residual noise and provide feedback to adapt the filter coefficients for improved cancellation under changing driving conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

A controller may generate a combination signal based on the sense signals and apply broadband filtering to the combination signal to produce a filtered reference signal representative of cabin noise over a selected frequency range. The controller may determine one or more anti-noise signals from the filtered reference signal using an adaptive control process and may drive one or more acoustic transducers in the vehicle cabin to generate anti-noise. The anti-noise may destructively interfere with road noise, engine noise, or a combination thereof at one or more listening positions in the cabin. In some examples, the broadband filtering and combination signal processing enable coordinated cancellation of both road and engine noise while reducing processing complexity and improving noise attenuation performance.
